name: Humanism
scope: Modern, organised humanism: the non-theistic, naturalistic, reason-and-ethics life stance and movement that the Amsterdam Declaration (1952, updated 2002 and 2022) of Humanists International calls the definitive statement of modern humanism, with the American Humanist Association's Humanist Manifestos (1933, 1973, 2003) and the accounts of Humanists UK, the AHA and Humanists International of what humanists hold, and the reference entry in the Encyclopedia of Science, Technology, and Ethics. It excludes Renaissance humanism (a classical-learning reform movement, per Britannica's entry), Christian humanism, Marxist humanism, existential humanism, Humanistic Judaism, humanistic psychology and 'secular humanism' in the narrower 1980 Declaration sense, each of which has its own subject or is a different use of the word; the Encyclopedia entry itself says these are 'different usages of the same word'.

summary: Humanism, as the organised movement states it (Humanists International's Amsterdam Declaration of 1952, 2002 and 2022; the American Humanist Association's Manifestos of 1933, 1973 and 2003; Humanists UK), is a non-theistic life stance. It holds that morality comes from human experience and needs no supernatural source, that reason and science are the way to solve human problems, and that every person has dignity and a right to the greatest freedom compatible with the rights of others. Politically it stands for democracy, civil liberties, equal rights, an impartial state separate from religion, and (in Manifesto II) a world community with international law and aid to poorer countries. It names no single economic system and asks that systems be judged by their results.
notes: Almost all statements are null: the defining sources are short statements of principle, and Manifesto II (1973) is the only text that takes positions on specific policy (sexuality, privacy, church and state, economics, world order, technology). Manifesto I (1933) calls for a 'socialized and cooperative economic order' while Manifesto II says the door is open to alternative systems and judges them by results, so public ownership is entered as a split. Searches of the saved sources for apostasy, blasphemy, capital punishment, same-sex marriage, sex education beyond the passage cited and drug policy found no stated position. The other humanisms (secular, Christian, Marxist, Humanistic Judaism) are separate ideologies and their sources were not used.
